name: Maison Dieu, Dover
text: Your train passes near the Maison Dieu, on the train's {side}, now the oldest part of Dover Town Hall. Hubert de Burgh, Constable of Dover Castle, founded it in 1203 as a hospital for pilgrims arriving from the Continent on their way to Becket's shrine at Canterbury.

name: St John's Church, Piddinghoe
text: Your train passes near St John's Church at Piddinghoe, across the River Ouse on the train's {side}. Its round Norman tower is one of three in the Ouse valley, the others being at Southease and St Michael's in Lewes.

name: Port of Newhaven
text: Your train passes the Port of Newhaven, on the train's {side}, where ferries sail to Dieppe in France. Newhaven was a fishing village of little importance as a port until the railway arrived in 1847.

name: Tide Mills
text: Your train passes near Tide Mills, on the train's {side}, a village beside a tide mill begun here in 1762. The village was condemned as unfit to live in in 1936 and abandoned in 1939.

name: St Leonard's Church, Seaford
text: Your train passes near St Leonard's Church, Seaford, on the train's {side}, parts of which are Norman work of the 11th century. In the Middle Ages Seaford was one of the main ports of southern England, but its harbour silted up and the French burned the town several times between 1350 and 1550.

name: Staines Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Thames on Staines Railway Bridge, completed in 1856. Its wrought iron girders rest on six cast iron pillars set in the river bed.

name: St Mary's Church, Staines
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Staines, on the train's {side}, standing on a rise above the Thames at the west end of the town. A plaque on its tower, built in 1631, says it was designed by Inigo Jones.

name: Saxon palace site, Old Windsor
text: Your train passes near the site of a palace of the Saxon kings at Old Windsor, on the train's {side}. Edward the Confessor held a royal manor here, and the palace was later replaced by the Norman castle at what became Windsor; Old Windsor was the first place to bear the name.

name: Datchet Bridge
text: Your train passes near where Datchet Bridge crossed the Thames, on the train's {side}. Berkshire and Buckinghamshire argued for decades over its upkeep, and in 1836 each built its own half, one in wood and one in iron, not touching in the middle. It was pulled down in 1848.

name: Eton College
text: Your train passes Eton College, on the train's {side}, founded by Henry VI in 1440. It is the largest boarding school in England, and has been called "the nurse of England's statesmen".

name: HM Prison Bronzefield
text: Your train passes HM Prison Bronzefield, on the train's {side}, the largest women's prison in Europe. The site was first a residential school for orphans from London, opened in 1872.

name: Mayflower Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Mayflower Theatre, on the train's {side}. It opened in 1928 as the Empire, and with seats for 2,300 it is the largest theatre in the south of England outside London.

name: St James' Church, Somerton
text: Your train passes near St James' Church in Somerton, on the train's {side}. In 1512 the Crown granted the manor to William Fermor, and in the 16th century the church's south aisle became the Fermor family's chapel.

name: Rousham House
text: Your train passes near Rousham House, on the train's {side}, built in about 1635 and attacked by Parliamentary soldiers in the Civil War. Its gardens were laid out by Charles Bridgeman and then by William Kent.

name: Port Meadow
text: Your train passes Port Meadow, on the train's {side}, a great stretch of common grazing land beside the Thames. The Freemen of Oxford's right to graze their animals here free of charge is recorded in the Domesday Book, and has been used ever since.

name: Radcliffe Observatory
text: Your train passes near the Radcliffe Observatory, on the train's {side}, Oxford University's observatory from 1773 until 1934. Its octagonal tower is based on the Tower of the Winds in Athens and is topped by a statue of Atlas holding up the world.

name: St Nicholas' Church, Islip
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas' Church in Islip, on the train's {side}. Edward the Confessor was born in Islip and baptised in a church here; the font is now at Middleton Stoney.

name: Alchester
text: Your train crosses the site of Alchester, a Roman town at a crossroads of Roman roads whose Roman name isn't known. Excavations have shown it was one of the earliest legionary fortresses in Britain after the invasion of AD 43.

name: Notley Abbey
text: Your train passes near the remains of Notley Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded for Augustinian canons in the 12th century and one of the richest in the Oxford area. Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh later owned it.

name: St Mary's Church, Ludgershall
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Ludgershall, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church dating from the 14th century. The Bible scholar John Wycliffe is reported to have been one of its early vicars.

name: St Mary's Church, Haddenham
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Haddenham, on the train's {side}, of 12th-century Norman origin. Haddenham is one of only three wychert villages in England, with walls built of white clay mixed with straw.

name: Church of St Mary and St Nicholas, Saunderton
text: Your train passes near Saunderton's church of St Mary and St Nicholas, on the train's {side}. It took its second saint in 1452, when the village's other church, St Nicholas, was pulled down After its walls began to lean in 1886 it was largely taken down and rebuilt.

name: The Mount, Princes Risborough
text: Your train passes near The Mount, on the train's {side}, now a car park but once the site of Risborough's royal manor house. The Black Prince was lord of the manor, and after his death the town became known as Prince Risberge, later Princes Risborough.

name: St Nicholas' Church, Great Kimble
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas' Church in Great Kimble, on the train's {side}. It was in this parish that John Hampden refused to pay his ship money in January 1636.

name: All Saints Church, Little Kimble
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church in Little Kimble, on the train's {side}. Inside are the remains of early 14th-century wall paintings of saints, among them St Francis preaching to the birds and a large St George.

name: Roman settlement at Fleet Marston
text: Your train passes the site of a Roman settlement at Fleet Marston, on the train's {side}, on the line of Akeman Street, the Roman road. In 2022 archaeologists working on HS2 found a Roman cemetery in the parish, with about 425 burials and 1,200 coins.

name: Stoke Mandeville Stadium
text: Your train passes near Stoke Mandeville Stadium, on the train's {side}, the National Centre for Disability Sport. It grew out of the Stoke Mandeville Games, the forerunner of the Paralympic Games, started in 1948 by the neurosurgeon Ludwig Guttmann at the hospital next door.

name: Stoke Mandeville
text: Your train passes near the village of Stoke Mandeville, on the train's {side}, whose name comes from the Norman de Mandeville family, first recorded here in 1284. Its old church stood alone a kilometre from the village; excavations for HS2 on its site found two Roman statues.

name: St Mary's Church, Wendover
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Wendover, on the train's {side}. Early Wendover seems to have been centred near the church, south of today's town centre; the town was granted a market charter in 1214.

name: Gipsy House
text: Your train passes near Gipsy House, on the train's {side}, the home of the writer Roald Dahl and his family for several decades. He and his wife, the actor Patricia Neal, bought it at auction for £4,500 in 1954.

name: Little Chalfont
text: Your train passes Little Chalfont, on the train's {side}, a village that grew up in the 20th century round its station. The station opened in 1889 as Chalfont Road, among isolated farms, and was renamed Chalfont & Latimer in 1915.

name: Buckinghamshire and Hertfordshire
text: Between Chalfont & Latimer and Chorleywood, your train passes from Buckinghamshire into Hertfordshire.
textReverse: Between Chorleywood and Chalfont & Latimer, your train passes from Hertfordshire into Buckinghamshire.

name: Hellfire Caves
text: Your train passes near the Hellfire Caves, on the train's {side}, man-made chalk and flint caverns running 260 metres into the hill above West Wycombe. They were dug between 1748 and 1752 for Sir Francis Dashwood, co-founder of the Hellfire Club, which met in them.

name: Wycombe Abbey
text: Your train passes near Wycombe Abbey, on the train's {side}, a girls' boarding school founded in 1896 by Dame Frances Dove. Its grounds of woods, gardens and a lake include a Cold War bunker.

name: Bekonscot
text: Your train passes near Bekonscot, on the train's {side}, a model village built in the 1920s by Roland Callingham at one inch to one foot, often called the oldest surviving model village in Britain. It helped inspire Enid Blyton.

name: Jordans Meeting House
text: Your train passes near Jordans, on the train's {side}, whose Quaker meeting house was built in 1688 and is one of the oldest in the country. William Penn, the founder of Pennsylvania, is buried in its burial ground.

name: Chalfont Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the M25 on the Chalfont Viaduct, five brick arches built between 1902 and 1906, long before the motorway passed beneath. A second, longer viaduct just to the west spans the A413.

name: Denham Place
text: Your train passes near Denham Place, on the train's {side}, a Dutch-style house built between 1688 and 1701 for Sir Roger Hill. Capability Brown landscaped its park in 1773, and later residents included members of the Bonaparte family and the American banker J. P. Morgan.

name: Bletchley Park
text: Your train passes near Bletchley Park, on the train's {side}, where codebreakers including Alan Turing broke the German Enigma and Lorenz ciphers during the Second World War.

name: Church of St Peter and St Paul, Kings Sutton
text: Your train passes near the church at Kings Sutton, on the train's {side}, whose spire, added in the late 14th century, rises to 198 feet (60 metres). Nikolaus Pevsner thought it "one of the finest, if not the finest, spire in this county of spires".
